subtopic: CONGRATULATION'S ON TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE MARRIAGE OF THEIR MAJESTIES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONGRATULATION'S ON TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE MARRIAGE OF THEIR MAJESTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members of the house are aware, our King and Queen are celebrating today their silver wedding anniversary. It will be the desire of all citizens of Canada to have congratulations and good wishes extended to Their Majesties on this occasion. I can think of no more appropriate manner of so doing than by resolutions of both houses of parliament conveying expressions of loyalty, devotion and affection toward the King and Queen from the people's representatives in parliament assembled.
I have had a word with my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Bracken), and he has kindly agreed to join with me in a resolution of which we have both approved, and which I shall move in just a moment. Let me only mention that never before in the history of our parliament has there been an occasion when it was possible to pass a congratulatory address upon the day of the silver wedding anniversary of the reigning sovereigns. When King George V and Queen Mary celebrated their twenty-fifth wedding anniversary the parliament of Canada was not in session. King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra celebrated their silver wedding anniversary before King Edward VII ascended the throne. Because of the untimely death of the Prince Consort which occurred before the twenty-fifth anniversary of the marriage of His Royal Highness to Queen Victoria there was no opportunity to extend such an address. These circumstances lend a note of added significance to the opportunity which is ours today. I am sure it is one that will be welcomed in all parts of our country, and by none more than by those of us who are representatives of the people in parliament.
I accordingly move, seconded by Mr. Bracken, the Leader of the Opposition:
That an humble address be presented to Their Majesties, the King and Queen, in the following words:
Most Gracious Sovereigns:
We, Your Majesties' loyal and dutiful subjects, the House of Commons of Canada in parliament assembled, beg to offer our sincere congratulations to Your Majesties on the 25th anniversary of your marriage.
As members of the Parliament of Canada, we are happy to avail ourselves of this anniversary to express the warmth of the feelings cherished towards Your Majesties by the Canadian people. Your devotion to each other, the exemplary character of your family life, and your unfailing consecration to public service through years alike of war and peace, have been an inspiration to your subjects everywhere.
We trust that Your Majesties may long be spared to share the happiness of life together, and to enjoy the affection of your peoples in all parts of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
I would ask that when this resolution is passed a copy of the resolution be cabled to Their Majesties by Your Honour, also that the cable be later supplemented by a copy of the resolution suitably engrossed and bound as a permanent memento of the expressions of the Canadian people toward Their Majesties, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth, at this time.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONGRATULATION'S ON TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE MARRIAGE OF THEIR MAJESTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion just moved by the Prime Minister is one with which I am sure every hon. member of this house will be in hearty agreement. I rise only to associate myself formally with it as seconder.
The silver wedding anniversary of our King and Queen serves to remind us that the crown in British commonwealth countries is one of the few remaining evidences of unity that we have, perhaps the best remaining one.
Fortunately the royal family has set us an example of family life and public service which has gained for them the respect and admiration of us all. At a time when certain political and social institutions are crumbling, and when other monarchies are falling, the British crown has emerged with a reputation enhanced throughout the world and more strongly enshrined in the hearts of the people than ever before.

Congratulations to Their Majesties
Under such circumstances-on behalf of my associates, and I am sure I speak, as the Prime Minister has done, for all members of the house-we join with all the other members in offering congratulations to the King and Queen on the twenty-fifth anniversary of their wedding, and in wishing for them many more years of life together in which to serve their people.

subtopic: CONGRATULATION'S ON TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE MARRIAGE OF THEIR MAJESTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition have spoken for all members of the house on this occasion, and we of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation wish to associate ourselves with the motion and the congratulations to Their Majesties.
May I take this opportunity of pointing out that a few days ago we celebrated another anniversary, that of the Prime Minister of Canada in exceeding the record of Sir Robert Walpole for long tenure of office as Prime Minister of Great Britain. What an extraordinary thing it is that throughout the last two centuries the British monarchy has remained a symbol of our unity and of the privileges and liberties which the parliaments of the commonwealth have won for us all. Because Their Majesties are symbolic of this unity and this great progressive democratic tradition, it is with pleasure that we join the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in this message of congratulations and good wishes.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to join with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in this expression of our good will and congratulations to Their Majesties the King and Queen on the twenty-fifth anniversary of their wedding day.
I speak for all in the Social Credit group when I say that we are deeply mindful of the high place which the King and Queen hold in the hearts of the people of this country and of the commonwealth as a whole. We wish for them long life and a continuation of the splendid example which as the royal family they have set to all the people of the commonwealth.
Motion agreed to.

EXPRESSION OP THANKS OP VISITING PARLIAMENTARIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a matter of privilege, in the name of those members who accepted the invitation of the board of trade of the City of Toronto through its worthy president, Mr. Hugh H. Lawson, to visit the Queen City under its auspices on the 24th and 25th of this month, I wish to take a few minutes of the time of the House of Commons to express the thankfulness and appreciation of the many members of the house, representing every province and every political group in this assembly, who accepted the invitation,
No expression of gratitude on my part could properly record our appreciation of the warm and cordial reception we were accorded by everyone, the friendliness of our hosts, and the interesting instructive program which most delightfully guided all our activities during our sojourn, and which was expertly scheduled and smoothly and beneficially implemented.
The same sentiments are also gratefully expressed to the mayor of Toronto, Mr. Hiram McCallum., and to the city of Toronto for their welcome and the banquet at which we were guests last Saturday evening.
Our thanks are also extended to the officials of the Toronto Transportation Commission for their most instructive demonstration dealing with civic improvements and rapid transit. Special mention should be made of the excellent transportation facilities which were provided for us and which we thoroughly enjoyed throughout the trip.
I should also like to express our most sincere appreciation to Mr. Thomas Rennie, former chairman of the Toronto Harbour Commission, and to the commission itself, for the information they provided us, the well-planned tour of the harbour by boat, and the luncheon given to us yesterday.
We express our most sincere gratitude also for the warm and gracious hospitality extended to us at a reception given by the Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario, Hon. Ray Lawson, and Mrs. Lawson, at their Oakville residence.
I also wish to express well deserved thanks to all the federal members representing the city of Toronto and adjacent districts, and their wives, for the courtesies and attentions they bestowed upon us on all occasions.
We cannot let this opportunity pass without making reference to one of our members who by his constructive contributions to civic and national welfare has left a deep imprint upon the hearts and minds of the citizens of his

Parliamentarians' Visit to Toronto
city, of which he had been the mayor for seven consecutive years; and he has been a active representative in this parliament almost continuously since 1921. We all realize that he is a peer among his people, and that he is held in the highest respect and affection by all. He was our constant companion, giving us practical and illuminating information on civic matters, and, by his wide experience and enthusiasm, inculcating in our minds a better knowledge and understanding of the problems and aspirations of the fine progressive people of the city he serves so well, in both the civic and the federal field. I refer, as all members know, to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church).
I feel that we should be remiss in our duty if we did not express to you, Mr. Speaker, our sincere admiration for the delicate, efficient and eloquent manner in which you expressed your sentiments when on several occasions you were called upon to speak. The spontaneous and prolonged applause you received in every instance from all your listeners was ample evidence of the impression made upon them by the words spoken by you in our behalf.
As a result of this journey we know that section of the country better than we did before, and there is no doubt that such contacts make all of us feel more friendly toward the people of the splendid city we had the good fortune to visit under such pleasant and efficient auspices, and a little closer to them than ever before.

We spent two delightful days in the city, well on into the evening and night, and those who were able to rise early on Sunday morning and go out and inspect the new Sunny-brook veterans hospital found it an experience well worthwhile.

HEALTH AND WELFARE-CHILD AND MATERNAL DIVISION-PUBLICATIONS
speechtext: What publications are distributed by the child and maternal health division o-f the Department of National Health and Welfare?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-CHILD AND MATERNAL DIVISION-PUBLICATIONS
speechtext:
No publications are distributed by the child and maternal health division of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The responsibility for the production and distribution of all health education material rests with the information services division of the department, and distribution of most books, pamphlets, folders, posters and other similar material is normally made through the provincial departments of health. Where the provincial departments have active divisions of health education the best possible use of such material can be made when it is placed in the hands of public health nurses and medical health officers who are directly in touch with the public, or when distributed through well-baby clinics, health units, child guidance clinics, etc., etc.
Many publications of the Department of National Health and Welfare have to do with the health and welfare of mothers and young children. Chief among such publications is the 232-page book "Canadian Mother and Child" written by the chief of the child and maternal health division, over 800,000 copies of which have been distributed to expectant mothers and others interested in child care.
Booklets, pamphlets and posters published by the department include the following:
"Healthful Living"; "Your Baby's Teeth"; "Your Child's Teeth".
Pamphlets dealing with dental hygiene;
"Polio": A leaflet dealing with infantile paralysis;
"Let's Talk Food Mother"; "Mother! The School Lunch". Pamphlets on nutrition.

"A Children's Charter". A booklet on Family Allowances in Canada.
A set of six posters on immunization.
A series of folders on child training, originally produced and distributed by the Canadian welfare council and now taken over by the Department of National Health and Welfare, is being revised and reprinted for general distribution through provincial channels. Already published are three in this series entitled:
[DOT] "Obedience: How Can I Teach My Child to Obey?" "Bed-Wetting: How Can I Correct My Child's Habit?" "Feeding Habits: How Can I Guide My Child's Eating?"
Three others in this series will be issued very shortly, as follows:
"Temper: How Can I Control My Child's Outbursts?" "Fear: What Makes My Child Afraid and Nervous?" "Sex:	What Should
I Tell My Child?"
A new folder devoted to child and maternal health, which will be appearing soon, is entitled "Ten Points to Remember-Before and After Baby Comes". This is intended as complementary material for distribution when the department's films on child and maternal health, "Mother and Her Child" and "Know Your Baby" and the filmstrips-"Nine to Get Ready" and "Introducing Baby" are being shown.

In view of the press reports on the judgment * of Chief Justice E. K. Williams of the Court of King's Bench of the province of Manitoba, in which the chief justice held invalid the powers exercised by the government with respect to barley under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, I desire to ask two questions. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in answer to the first question, instructions have been given to appeal from the judgment of Chief Justice Williams. The authority of the governor in council to pass a certain order in council appropriating properly was denied in the judgment of Mr. Justice Williams. But I am not aware of any prejudicial effect upon any other controls.

speechtext:
Hon. COLIN GIBSON (Secretary' of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 198, to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1938.
He said: This bill, Mr. Speaker, is to be referred to a special committee of the house after second reading. A special committee has been set up to consider it.
Mr. JOHN R. MacNICOL (Davenport): I know it is to be referred to the committee, Mr. Speaker, but is it in order to make comments at this time?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Certainly.
Dominion Elections Act

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I will not be long, Your Honour. I have had a great deal to do with election acts. I am thoroughly familiar with the election acts of all the democracies, particularly those of the British empire. I am glad to say that on the whole the Dominion Elections Act, which came from the committee and is going back there, is in my opinion the best election act in any of our democracies. I do not say it is perfect, but it is better than any other act in operation in any component part of the British empire. It is a monument to our chief electoral officer, who has studied election acts more than anyone else I know of. He was a very great help to the committee, as was also the chairman. I did not notice the hon. gentleman in the house, but I can repeat that statement. He was an excellent chairman and kept the committee going forward all the time.
I might mention just one or two things the act does, which lead me to say it is a most excellent piece of legislation. In some parts of Canada when an election occurs we may have both fast and slow time. The act now makes it specific that at all times during an election standard time governs. I believe that is something new.
The part of the act dealing with advance polls has been improved to permit sailors, mounted policemen and government officials who are to be absent on government work, to use them, all of which should have been done in previous acts. It seems to me that for years * the chief electoral officer has been keeping notes of things that should be done to bring the act right up to the minute, and so far as I have observed he has not left out anything. It was not his fault we did not adopt the Quebec system of manning and conducting the polls. I brought up the matter, but the committee did not see fit to adopt the suggestion. I believe it would have been an improvement, and when the act is again revised I hope the Quebec system will be followed. There the government of the day names the returning officer, while the party receiving the next highest vote names the clerk. I have advocated that for years in this house. I am not now going to complain because my suggestion was not adopted; I am satisfied to let it go through as it is, but on another occasion I hope we may be big enough and broad enough to adopt this change. It simply means that you take politics right out of the polls, and it would obviate the necessity of other parties having scrutineers, because with two parties represented there would not be much chance of crooked work.
Another provision in the act permits all lapanese who served in our forces during the

last war to vote. Not only that; they are accorded the same privilege that our own people are given, namely that their wives may vote as well. I am convinced that this is a step in the right direction. The same thing applies to Indians, of whom several thousand served in the last war. Those Indians and their wives are also permitted to vote. The Indian committee has not yet reported to the house; we do not know what they will recommend in reference to permitting all Indians to vote, so I am not going to offer any comment on that at the moment.
Another clause permits all veterans of the late war under twenty-one years of age at the time of the election to vote. I believe that also is a step in the right direction. Perhaps by the time an election comes along there will not be any veterans less than twenty-one years of age; but if there are, they too will be able to vote.
Another section deals with students at universities or colleges. If they are registered at the university or college on the day of the issue of the writ they will have the privilege of registering to vote either in their home ridings or at the university or college they are attending. In the past many students have been barred from voting merely because they were away from home at the time of the enumeration.
Another provision which I think is very good pertains to soldiers in hospitals. A soldier is allowed to choose whether he will register in the riding in which the hospital is located or have his vote transferred to his home riding.
One section perhaps will need some amending; that is the section which refers to contract workers away from home. I know the chief electoral officer has been written to about it. At the moment it is not quite clear, but I am satisfied the committee will rectify that and make it possible for persons working in ridings in which by-elections are to be held, to vote there if they were residing in that riding at the time of the issue of the writ.
I like the section referring to enumerators; it really is to the credit of the chief returning officer. When the enumeration is taking place two enumerators shall be appointed, one by (he government of the day and one by the party which had the next highest number of votes in that riding. This will not mean that all parties will be represented in the enumeration, but one of the enumerators will be appointed by the government and the other bv one of the other .parties; and the act has been amended to provide that the enumerators will have to do their job. We had instances in connection with the enumeration in the last election where one of the two enumerators

Dominion Elections Act
might say, "I have to go down town for the afternoon. You go ahead with the enumeration." That sort of thing will be stopped now, and the enumerators will be compelled to go in pairs and staj' on the job until it is done properly. This is another step in the right direction.
I want to say just a word about the riding of Yukon-Mackenzie, though I do not know whether we can do anything about it. We did thresh out that question thoroughly in committee, but we were not unanimous on it. Some of us felt that Yukon-Mackenzie is really an impossible riding for size. It covers over 700,000 square miles and consists of two very large areas. The activities of Yukon are not in any way related to the activities of the Mackenzie district, and there is no connection between them by air, road or railway. I cannot see how in the world any candidate can contest that riding. I have been over it myself, and I know. You cannot go straight through the Mackenzie area to Yukon. I flew there in a powerful American plane. It had to go over two high ranges of mountains, flying sometimes at an altitude of eight to nine thousand feet, and I do not think ordinary commercial planes can do that. Anyone going from the Yellowknife to the Yukon would have to go away south and then come north again; therefore I do not know how in the world the candidates contesting an election in the Yukon-Mackenzie riding can get around the riding.
The people in that area are strongly opposed to this. I am not speaking now in the expectation that anything can be done, but I would remind the house that a census will be taken in 1951, only three years hence. Then there will be a redistribution, and I hope that at that time the committee dealing with redistribution will give direct representation to the people in the Mackenzie district, as well as to those in the Yukon. As I said, the people up there are opposed to these two areas being put together.
I think I should place on Hansard what the local paper in Yellowknife has to say. I should like to quote from the Yellowknife Blade of April 5, 1948, the editor of which is .John Murray McMeekan. He has been a stout advocate of separate representation for these two areas.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope that the committee will deal with the section relating to Indians and Eskimos. Five thousand of these men fought in the first world war and even more in the second. They should be treated as human beings and given the full rights of citizens. I hope that when the committee considers the bill this section will be dealt with.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister has said that this bill will be referred to the committee, but I am almost certain that I shall not be a member of that committee. I have glanced over the bill and I cannot find any provision for the transferable vote in single constituencies. This has been a strong contention of mine, although I know that some hon. members do not agree with me.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: I am absolutely opposed to it. I hope there will never be anything like that in the Dominion Elections Act.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I want to repeat what I have said in many past sessions and point out what may be the result in this country if we do not make provision for the transferable vote in single constituencies. In the federal election of 1940 seventy-four members out of 245 were returned to this house with minority votes of their constituencies. In the 1945 general election approximately 150 members out of 245 were returned to this house with minority votes in their constituencies. I submit that before a member is finally declared elected he or she should have in the transfer at least a majority of the votes cast in the riding.
This principle has been in operation for many years in Manitoba and I believe also in Alberta. If anyone wishes to study the acts and how they work out he can confer with the officials in those provinces.
Dominion Elections Act

I trust that the members of the committee which will be studying the act will consider this matter very seriously.
I can picture the possibility in the future of a government coming into office after obtaining only a small percentage of the votes cast. I am democratic enough to say that I would be satisfied if even an extreme socialist government came into power provided they had obtained a majority of the votes cast at the time they were elected. I do not think we should make it possible for a government to be brought into power with perhaps only a quarter or a third of the votes cast. I am thinking of the years ahead when such a thing might easily be possible.
I hope that the members of this committee will give serious consideration to providing for the transferable vote in single constituencies.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few words to say on the second reading of this bill. While we in this corner generally approve most of the amendments provided by this bill, we were disappointed last year because the voting age was not reduced to eighteen years. I hope that the committee which is to consider the bill will reconsider its attitude in this particular matter and provide that the age qualification be so reduced.
I shall repeat in committee the plea which I made last year in this particular regard. I feel that persons eighteen years of age who are old enough to don a uniform and fight for this country ought to be considered old enough to exercise the franchise. Since the government has the power in an emergency to declare that these young people must fight for their country, I feel that these same young people should have some voice in the selection of the government which has that authority.
I hope that this matter will receive more favourable consideration this year than it was given last year. The committee which was set up last year to review these amendments did a very good job. They worked long hours over a considerable period, and on the whole, with a few minor exceptions, what the committee accomplished was approved by our group. But I hope the one point I have mentioned will be given careful consideration this year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I rise to put on record some suggestions which have been sent to me by one of my constituents who might be described as a shut-in. He is, however, a man who despite some physical handicaps has achieved considerable and commendable success in the business world. He has spoken to me on.behalf of those who are
[Mr. Ross (Souris)P
handicapped or shut in. His name is R. S. Macdonald, and I should like to put before the minister one or two of his suggestions so that they may be considered by the committee.
The first is that the directions to district returning officers should be published in two booklets, one for urban and another for rural constituencies. This would make it easier for new returning officers to familiarize themselves with their duties without having to search through a long and cumbersome instruction booklet.
A second suggestion is that a candidate's party should be mentioned under his name on the ballot, and that he should be permitted to label himself as the official candidate of his party. I believe that that suggestion is a good one, especially in these times when we have as many as eight candidates in a constituency. Some voters are anxious to support a party with whose principles they agree, but they are confused when they find eight or ten names on the ballot.
Another suggestion is that some effort be made by the returning officers to clarify the occupation of the candidate. For instance, after a candidate's name there might be just the word "president". He might be president of anything. Perhaps the returning officers could be given instructions in that regard.
His final suggestion, and this is the one for which I particularly plead today, is that the enumerators be instructed to take the names of shut-ins, bedridden voters, who have no chance of ever getting to the poll. He suggests that when the enumerator calls at a house he ask if there are any shut-ins or bedridden people there, and that the enumerator make a separate list of such people for the returning officer, who could then mail each of them a ballot before election day. The shut-ins could mark their choice of a candidate and return the ballot in. the self-addressed envelope sent by the returning officer. The returning officer would know how many ballots he had sent out by mail and could check that number against the numbers that come in, to prevent any voting by ineligible persons. He would then credit the ballots to the proper candidates and deposit them in the box.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was a member of the committee in 1936, 1937 and 1938 when the Dominion Elections Act was being overhauled, and a pretty good job was done at that time. I also was on the committee which dealt with the Dominion Elections Act in wartime. That committee w7as on a non-political basis. Again last year we spent many days making minor changes in the elections act, and I do not

Dominion Elections Act
know whether we have had any more friendly committee than that one.
I understand that this bill is to be referred to a committee for consideration. So far, few fundamental changes have been suggested, but there is one which I think should be made to ensure that the candidate returned will have a greater proportion of the votes of his constituency than often happens at the present time.
In Alberta we have in the rural ridings what is called the single transferable vote. I think we could very well adopt that s\-stem, in the rural ridings at least, for the purposes of the Dominion Elections Act. At the present time, where you have five candidates running in a constituency, one may get only twenty-one per cent of the total vote and yet be elected to parliament. I do not believe that is good business, either for the candidate himself or for the country. I suggest that the government or the committee do something to remedy that unsatisfactory situation.
I hope that when the committee meets we shall all use the best judgment of which we are capable in dealing with the amendments which come before us.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to endorse what the hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. Fair) has just said. In Alberta we have had the single transferable vote for a long time, and in Manitoba too, and I have never in all these years heard a single complaint about it. Most people confuse it with what is known as proportional representation, but that is not the same thing at all. The single transferable vote simply means that we do what we do at a political convention which is electing a candidate, where the low man is dropped and his votes transferred until finally the person elected is bound to have fifty per cent of the votes plus one. If that system were adopted in our federal elections it would mean that the candidate elected would not be a minority representative. I am one myself, though not by very many votes; nevertheless I am.
I do not see how we can continue to talk about the grand principle of majority rule when the most of us who are here-150 of us, I am informed by an hon. member-are here without the support of the majority of the people within our ridings. There were five candidates in my riding, and on that basis a person could be elected, theoretically, we will say, with one-fifth of the vote plus one. I do hope that the committee will give consideration to the suggestion.
There is one other matter, and only one, that I wish to mention. I have not read the bill, but I do not think it contains a provision to enable permanently disabled persons to vote. I may say that being very much interested in this matter I communicated with the chief electoral officer. All of us I think will realize the justice of it, and it is only a matter of working out a rule or the conditions under which this could be done. I have had not many letters-I have had three

from my own home city, with respect to three persons there. I should not tell you their politics, sir, but perhaps you may be able to guess it; so I am helping myself to that extent.
But leaving that sort of thing out, it might be impossible at the moment in some constituencies which are far-flung and sparsely settled. It might present difficulties there but it seems to me some arrangement could be made by which we could carry the ballot to the person. It would not be a very expensive matter. I think I represent about half the city of Calgary. I am quite sure that so far as numbers go it would merely mean the employment of one or two persons and one motorcar for the day of the election.
I merely make the suggestion, sir, in order that the committee may examine it and see if it is not-to borrow the expression I hear from my friends to my left-physically possible to permit these people to exercise their franchise.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to endorse the principle of the single transferable vote. When I was first returned to the House of Commons I was a minority member; I won a majority of all the votes at the general election. There is no guarantee that that situation will prevail, therefore in passing I should like to say that I believe it is fair and democratic and would result in returning the people's choice as their representative in the House of Commons.
My principal object in rising is to speak for a moment on behalf of the Canadian Indian. I have served on the Indian affairs committee for three years and I know there is a sense of fear on the part of the Indians themselves in seeking the franchise. They fear that they might be required to give up some of their treaty rights. The Indian was disqualified partly because he enjoys exemption from taxation. We all know of the mounting taxes which we have today. His exemption was on the land on the reserve, and is his by treaty right. But today the average Indian contributes a great deal in taxes. He pays the eight per cent sales tax; he pays the tax on gasoline, and a multitude of other taxes. On
Dominion Elections Act

the money he earns off the reserve he is subject also to income tax. The evidence presented before the Indian affairs committee has indicated a still further desire on his part to be relieved from the income tax; and yet some of them are making substantial incomes. It seems fair to say that if they are to work off the reserve and take the. place of one who might otherwise earn this income, they should be subject to income tax. However, I am prepared to say this: if we were to grant them the right to vote in the dominion or provincial elections it would be educational in itself. It would break down the feeling of inferiority, and I do believe it 'can be done in a practical way; that is to say, I can imagine that some of the Indians living in the more remote areas, where they might be considered more or less primitive people still, might not have the necessary qualifications to exercise the franchise. But I do believe the act can be so worded that the Indian on an Indian reserve within or adjacent to certain electoral districts, where the Department of Indian Affairs are acquainted with their standard of education and their educational facilities, could be given the franchise.
These reserves are all well known. The Indians should be given the franchise because, as I have already said, they are making a sizeable contribution in taxation to the national exchequer and to the provincial government as well. The Indian is not prepared to accept this if it means giving up any of his rights, and yet one of the principal objects of our committee is to encourage the Indian to become a full-fledged citizen, prepared to accept his full responsibility. Such a move would be a step in the right direction if he knew in the beginning that he was not giving up any of his ancient rights to enjoy the franchise.
As the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) said, these people made a tremendous contribution in both wars. I can think of the reserve adjacent to my own riding, Cape Croker, where their enlistment on a per capita basis was far greater than that of any other community I know of, and many of them made the supreme sacrifice. I realize that provision is made here for the Indian veteran to vote, and I am pleased to see an amendment to the act to permit that Indian's wife to vote. I hope that in considering this bill the committee will give serious consideration to the suggestions I have made with respect to the Indian reserves adjacent to or within electoral districts, where in the opinion of the Department of Indian Affairs the inhabitants of that reserve have reached such u xatis-

factory level of culture and development that they might exercise intelligently the franchise, even if in the beginning it is granted only to male Indians. There is a degree of backwardness amongst some of the women which I think could be corrected in due time through the educational advantages they are enjoying. In the beginning the franchise might be granted much on the same basis as we first enjoyed it, and after a time the women could be included, to make the job complete.
I want to say a word as to the suggestion offered by the members of the C.C.F. party with respect to young persons eighteen years of age. I have never been able to support this view. All too soon the burdens of national responsibility fall upon the shoulders of these young people. I wonder whether my hon. friend appreciates entirely what the franchise means or should mean. If we provide the franchise to the eighteen year olds, along with that franchise should go the responsibility of citizenship, the responsibility for debt, the responsibility of being sued in a court of law and subject to judgment being executed against him if one was obtained; the right to hold a liquor permit, the right to frequent beverage rooms and cocktail lounges, and everything else. I doubt whether we are prepared to go that far.
So far as the young men who enlisted are concerned, I can look back and take this view. I know that the young man of seventeen or eighteen who is full of enthusiasm, healthy and robust in physique, venturesome and willing to take a chance, would make an ideal soldier under the leadership that is provided for him. Because some of our greatest airmen were willing to venture and take a chance they made great names for themselves. The same thing applies to men in other branches of the armed services. But provision is already made in this act that even if the soldier were discharged from the armed forces, because of his enlistment he would still be entitled to the franchise irrespective of what his age might be when the election was called. Someone might say:	Well, that
will soon pass away; but I would be more impressed by the advantages of extending the franchise if those who now enjoy that right would roll out to the polls in greater numbers and exercise their right to vote. In other words, unless we can encourage our people to believe that the franchise holds something of advantage for them; unless we can impress upon them the great instrument the ballot really is and have them vote in larger numbers than thirty or forty or fifty per cent, why extend the franchise to those of younger years?-although I must say in my own riding

in both the by-election and the general election we polled well over seventy per cent of the eligible voters.
Of course, as the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey) has said, there are those who are shut in and unable to get to the polls. I am not prepared to say we should call for compulsory voting at this time, but I do believe that through the educational approach we should try to impress upon our young people the advantages the franchise offers. As the parent of young children I cannot think of anything of greater importance.
I believe that a man reaches mature judgment-I do not know that I would use that word literally, but certainly he reaches a stage of better judgment at twenty-five years than at twenty-one. I question very much if the youth of our land are prepared to accept this responsibility, subject to a poll tax and all the other obligations which go with it, at eighteen years of age.
I do not believe I have anything further to say, except to leave my appeal with the committee with respect to the Canadian Indian.

Of course not in the same ridings; you could not have proportional representation in a one-man riding. But the purpose is the same. The single transferable vote provides that before a person is elected he must have a majority of the votes cast. When the votes are counted the low candidates are counted out and the second and third choice go to the candidates in the field. That is continued until one person receives a majority of the votes cast.
It is interesting to note that this question of the single transferable vote has come to have such importance in the country at this time. I have been interested in proportional representation for many years and have advocated it. If we are to have the single transferable vote in one-member constituencies 1 suggest that in urban constituencies, where constituencies can be bunched, we have proportional representation.
I say that because there are two important points in connection with representation in parliament. One is that as nearly as possible the government in office should have a majority of the people behind it. The second is that significant groups within the country should have representation in parliament and in the legislatures in proportion to their members. Let me point this out, that with the single transferable vote, although every member elected might have a majority of the votes in his constituency, yet a government could be elected with the minority of the votes in the country. Consequently we may not be any farther ahead than we are at the present time.

Dominion Elections Act

that I personally am a minority representative, having received I think forty-four or forty-five per cent of the votes cast, I still believe the single transferable vote would complicate our voting procedure and furthermore would lend itself to a duplication of candidates with complex instructions to the electors how to cast the second vote. From the point of view of my own constituency, which is a large industrial constituency in Ontario, I see nothing but complication, confusion and a general lack of efficiency in the taking of a vote under this system.
I have not had any experience with the single transferable vote or with proportional representation, but I must also oppose proportional representation because almost always you find that the man whose name heads the ballot stands the greatest chance of election. So much is this the case that in many instances the names are jumbled alphabetically after every thousand or so ballots, so the people will not be influenced by the names at the top of the list and vote as they really wish. Proportional representation may be all very well for those of us whose names begin with the early letters of the alphabet, but I feel that individual contact between the elector and the candidate for whom he wishes to vote is the important contact to maintain. To confuse the matter by complicating the electoral machinery would, I think, not give as direct representation as we have at the present time, despite the faults in the present system which many of us in this house recognize.
I should like to mention one other matter which has to do with the boundaries of constituencies bordering cities, though I do not think it comes under the Representation Act. Certainly this matter concerns the four York ridings and probably a number of others contiguous to metropolitan areas. In almost all cases, for the purpose of constructing streets, the city boundary does not run down the centre line of a street bordering a city. The city boundary runs one lot, or sixty feet, behind the outside edge of the street. In other words, in the case of York West, people living in the front of an apartment house on Bloor street will vote in the city riding of High Park, while those across the hall in the same apartment building will vote in the county riding of York West. I want to suggest that this anomaly should be corrected, if at all possible. Certainly it confuses a great many voters who live in apartment houses, part of which are in one riding and part in another. Despite the fact that the city boundaries are not the same as the boundaries

of the ridings, I suggest that, in order to simplify the matter, whenever possible the centre street line be used as the constituency boundary.
Then I should like to add one word to the remarks of the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Case) with respect to the eighteen-year-old having a liquor permit, and so on. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis) pounced upon that, which I suppose was to be expected; but the point is, are you going to make the eighteen-year-old, who is in many cases a high school student, a legal entity? Are- you going to make him capable of being sued and responsible for debt before the courts? Are you prepared to do that or are you not? That was the important question raised by the hon. member for Grey North, and it is an issue which I think should be decided. There is no question that the man who enlisted and fought obviously must be given the vote. That question is not pertinent at the moment, however, because the war has been over for a considerable period of time and those who fought in it will now be over the age of twenty-one.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks, which I hope will bring about comments in one direction or another. In this country we have a strong belief that we live in a real democracy which is endowed with the best in the way of democratic institutions. That statement is probably as true and accurate in Canada as it would be anywhere else, but is it as true and accurate as it might be?
Many definitions have been given of democracy, some at variance with others. It is hard to decide which definition best serves the purpose; but perhaps a common one is as good as any other; that is, government of the people, by the people, for the people. "By the people" of course means the majority of the people, particularly those who express their views on the proper occasion.- People have the opportunity to express their views through agencies such as the radio, the press and different bodies and organizations, but by far the most efficient and decisive manner in
Dominion Elections Act

which the people can express their opinion is through the ballot on the occasion of an election.
Since this unique opportunity of a general election does not arise very often, it is of the utmost importance that we should have a government faithfully reflecting the opinion and views of the majority. Great care should be taken to see that the general expression of opinion given at a general election shall be given with the greatest possible degree of freedom.
In order to make democracy workable, this greatest possible degree of freedom in the marking of the ballot should be followed up with an equal degree of freedom when the elected representatives of the people are called upon to cast their votes on the floor of the house. In this debate I cannot discuss this latter aspect of the problem of the freedom of the vote on the floor of the house except to the limited extent to which it may be met through amendments to the Dominion Elections Act. I may, later on, refer to it.
Let me first deal with the suggestion which in my opinion would lead to a freer and more accurate expression of opinion on election day. This could be brought about only through further amendments to the elections act. In the first place, there is a serious problem, the matter of election costs to candidates or to whoever supplies the campaign funds. Campaign funds are no secret. It is a fact publicly known to the people of this country, and it has been admitted, without great criticism. But I think today we are beginning to meet more criticism on that aspect of our democratic institutions. I feel that I could put up a fairly good case to defend and justify this modern institution of campaign funds. I am prepared to admit that there are two aspects of the problem. At the same time, in an academic discussion or in a public forum I think I would rather defend the other view, namely, that party funds should be eliminated. This need not necessarily affect personal contributions coming from personal friends of the candidate within the county. I think there would be no great objection to that provided that fact were known to the public.
In order to bring about this much needed reform, I feel that the elections act should be amended in many respects, and in such a way as to provide under the act for more financial assistance to candidates. With that object in view, I should like to suggest that the elections act be amended in such a way as (1), to pay reasonable remuneration to the election agents of all candidates, not more than one per poll; <2) to pay reasonable amounts for publicity,

be it through radio, the press or otherwise; (3) to pay reasonable expenses for the use of halls and travelling expenses. What are reasonable expenses for radio, the press, halls, and so forth, would depend to a large extent upon the size of the constituency, its locality, the density of its population and the publicity agencies therein.
In order to offset to some extent this increase in election costs, I would urge that the amount of the deposit of candidates be raised from $200 to $1,000. This would discourage straw or nuisance candidates. I would urge that deposits of unsuccessful candidates be disposed of on a slightly more equitable basis. Refunds could be made on the basis of a percentage of the votes obtained by each unsuccessful candidate as compared with the total number of votes collected by the successful candidate. For instance, suppose that the elected candidate received 10,000 votes and the runner-up 8,000; the runner-up receiving 8,000 would be entitled to a refund of 80 per cent of his deposit. Another candidate receiving 4,000 votes would be entitled to a refund of 40 per cent of his deposit, and one receiving 1,000 votes would be entitled to only a 10 per cent refund of his deposit. If that principle had prevailed in the 1945 election the government would have collected larger amounts of forfeited money. For instance, in the constituency of Verdun forfeited deposits would have amounted to $7,800, instead of $1,800. In the constituency of Vancouver South they would have amounted to $3,240 instead of $800, and finally in my own riding of Restigouche-Madawaska forfeited moneys would have amounted to $2,200 instead of $600. I submit that these sums would go a long way toward the payment of the additional election expenses which I have just advocated.
On the other hand, this deposit of $1,000 required from each candidate would not constitute an undue burden on him because he would receive considerably more than that amount for his benefit in the nature of paid publicity and other election expenses. At the same time this larger deposit would act as a deterrent to straw or nuisance candidates, such as the one we had in the Glengarry byelection.

The time has come when this matter of election funds should be looked into a little further. subtopic: PROVISIONAL AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 35, respecting the provisional fur seal agreement between Canada and the United States.
Mr. W. CHESTER S. McLURE (Queens): Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few brief remarks concerning this bill, about the principle of which I have spoken on several other occasions.
This bill has for its purpose the carrying out of the pelagic sealing provisions between Canada and the United States, as set out in the agreements of 1942 and 1947. The bill represents something more than the mere carrying out of those agreements. Its purpose is to put into the Pelagic Sealing Act such teeth as for the future will assure both the United States and Canada that pelagic sealing will be a thing of the past.
I am not going into the history of the fur seal trade, because there are other hon. members who will discuss that part of the subject. I would point out, however, that the United States purchased Alaska in 1867 and, as they term it, made the greatest territorial purchase or bargain ever known to the world. At that time they paid for Alaska $7,200,000 and, while it was a large territory about one-fifth the size of the United States, there came with it a herd of fur seals numbering almost four million. This then was the property of the United States. There were, however, entanglements with other countries bordering that area. These have been dispensed with through the years.
After the purchase in 1867 by the United States, nothing was done in connection with maintaining the herd until about 1911. It was found that, because of extensive pelagic sealing, from 1867 the herd of about four million had been reduced to 125,000. The danger facing them at that time was the extinction of this great fur seal trade of Alaska.
Provisional Fur Seal Agreement

In 1911 the English, the Russians, the Japanese and the United States governments put into effect a treaty which gave the United States entire control of the seal herd of Alaska. Today there are only two partners, Canada and the United States. The United States get 80 per cent of the herd seal pelts that are taken off each year, and Canada is entitled to 20 per cent. If we do not have a proper, strong Pelagic Sealing Act that will take care of this great, industry, Canada's 20 per cent will not be worth much to her in years to come. That is one reason why I hope the committee of the whole, in going over this act, will examine every part of it in order to make it as strong as possible, both in our own interests and in those of the United States.
Since 1911 the United States have taken over one million pelts or skins, which have brought in to them more than twelve times the amount they paid for the whole of Alaska and the fur sealing trade.
One more thing I wish to emphasize in reference to this matter is that today we have more interest shown in the House of Commons with regard to the fur seal trade than we have had for a good many years. Interest is being taken in it because it produces quite a large revenue to the fisheries department of our government. I might say that at the present time, even when furs in general are at a little lower price, the recent sale of furs which was held on April 19 showed that the three types of seal skins, in which Canada as well as the United States, has an interest, sold at wonderfully good prices, even under today's fur depression as we might call it.
The dyeing and processing of these fur seal skins is done in two different countries: London, England, and St. Louis, Missouri. During the war the processing was not as good in London as it had been in St. Louis, because of conditions over which they had no control. However, the processing in St. Louis has developed so much that today it is acknowledged to be finest processing system for seal skins anywhere in the world, and this is shown by the three classes of skins they process, machine and dye. The skins are put out in three colours: safari, matara and black. The black is a glossy skin, and in the last sale averaged some $47. The safari is a unique kind of colour. It might be called a rich seal brown. It nearly held the spotlight, and averaged $65 per skin. The matara is a kind of neutral colour, brown with a bluish cast, and in the sale of some 10,000 skins it averaged S75 per pelt. I mention this just because Canada is greatly interested today. Some
5,000	skins are today being processed in St. Louis. Three thousand of them have arrived

in Montreal already, and will be sold at an early day-some time in June-for the benefit of the fur manufacturers of Canada.
In connection with this I might also say that the government or the fisheries department at the present time stand in the position that, by looking carefully into this industry, they have and can have a net revenue of at least a million dollars a year. Perhaps some of it may be swallowed up in duty on the skins coming into Canada because, when these skins go to St. Louis to be processed and are brought back into Canada, the national revenue department take away from the fisheries department some 12-[ per cent by way of duty. However, it is just going into a different pocket in the government.
Although I am not quite certain as to the amount, I think the cost of processing these skins is somewhere around $14 per skin. If I am wrong in this the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacKinnon) will correct me. It may be a little more or a little less. What I wanted to say in reference to the matter is this. We might in the future consider a proposition to have the processing done in Canada. The only way we might approach it is to ask the fur company in St. Louis to place an extra factory in Canada for processing our share of these pelts.
Again I want to repeat that in this act there are some things which might be made a little bit more drastic. For instance, I notice that, under certain conditions, certain individuals living in the north-the aborigines, the Aleuts and others-are allowed the right themselves to take on pelagic sealing. Personally I think that when we come to committee of the whole, those are things which we should look into carefully. As I said at the beginning, let us put all the teeth we possibly can into this act in order to save one of the greatest industries in the fur trade of Canada.
Hon. J. A. MaoKINNON (Minister of Fisheries) : I had intended, Mr. Speaker, to make a short statement on second reading of this bill. However, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) got ahead of me for the moment. Before making this statement, I should like to compliment him' on the speech he has just made, and for the knowledge he shows he has with regard to the sealing industry.
While my statement is short, it is longer than might be required under this bill; because, as far as I know, and as far as I can see, there is little of a contentious nature in it. But in making the statement I want to anticipate questions that might be asked me later.
The purpose of this bill is to carry out Canada's obligations under the provisional fur

Provisional Fur Seal Agreement
seal agreement made between Canada and the United States in 1942. The terms of this agreement are printed as schedule A of this measure.
In 1911 an agreement was reached to regulate, by international action, the killing of fur seals in the north Pacific. In that year Canada, acting through the United Kingdom, entered into the first pelagic sealing convention with the United States, Russia and Japan. All parties observed the terms of this convention until 1941. As a result of its abrogation by the Japanese government, this initial agreement came to an end about the time of Japan's entry into the second world war.
Canada and1 the United States were anxious to continue their joint efforts to preserve and protect the seal herds. A provincial fur seal agreement was therefore entered into by our two countries in 1942. But the Canadian legislation giving effect to this agreement was based on the War Measures Act. This meant, of course, that the life of the agreement was subject to a definite time limit. Accordingly the purpose of this bill is to enact legislation extending the life of the 1942 agreement for an indefinite period.
In the main, provisions of the original 1911 international convention are incorporated in the present Canadian-United States agreement. The principal changes may be briefly summarized as follows:
(a)	An increase in the Canadian share of fur seal skins taken annually at Pribilof islands from 15 per cent to 20 per cent.
(b)	A provision for enabling pelagic sealing under emergency circumstances. Details regarding conditions under which such emergency sealing might be conducted and the sharing of seal skins so taken are to be the subject of consultation between the two governments.
(c)	A provision for permitting the taking of fur seals for purposes of scientific research.
(d)	A provision that the two governments consult from time to time regarding the level of population at which the seal herd is to be maintained or other important phases of management or policy.
I do not propose to review in detail the extensive and interesting background of this sealing question. Briefly, the situation is that the breeding grounds of the fur seals are located on islands in the north Pacific. The seals breed during summer months and then swim to about the latitude of southern California before returning to the islands in the spring. The term "pelagic sealing" refers to the killing or capture of these fur seals at sea when they are migrating to and from their northern breeding grounds.
An international agreement was necessary in order to prevent the complete extinction of
these seals from the effects of unrestricted slaughter. In 1867, when the United States took over Alaska, there were nearly five million such seals. By 1911 the population had dropped to less than 125,000. By 1947, as a result of conservation measures, this number had increased to 3,600,000. These figures speak for themselves.
Canadian revenues as a result of the treaty and under its provisions have amounted to $5,482,141.15 since 1912. The consolidated revenue fund of Canada benefits in the following manner. Every fifth barrel of raw skins obtained by the United States government at the breeding grounds is stencilled for Canada. The skins are brought to Seattle by the United States and shipped from there to London, England, or to St. Louis in proportions governed by the decision of the Canadian government. When the skins are dressed and dyed at these centres they are returned to Canada for sale in Montreal through the Canadian Fur Auction Sales Company, which acts as government agent in these transactions. The proceeds, as I have indicated, go to the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
The provisions of this bill follow closely the contents of the Pelagic Sealing Act of 1938 enacted by this parliament to carry out the terms of the 1911 convention. The 1938 legislation came to an end, of course, as a result of the abrogation of the treaty in 1941. The only changes made by this bill are those required by a few modifications of the original 1911 agreement and the necessity for clarification on some minor points.
There is one principal exception to the restrictions imposed by the treaty. This relates to the provision that pelagic sealing may be carried on by Indians and other aborigines dwelling on the coasts of the waters to which the agreement refers. These sealing operations so permitted must, however, be carried on by means of canoes and without the use of firearms. These conditions are provided, because the existence of any large scale catching or killing equipment in the hands of the exempted persons might well open the door to serious abuses.
These are the main provisions of the legislation now before the house. I should add that Canada, under the treaty arrangement, undertakes to give the United States 20 per cent of any seals captured on Canadian territory.

subtopic: PROVISIONAL AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Is Russia under the agreement?

subtopic: PROVISIONAL AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Russia is not under the agreement. As a matter of fact, however, practically no seals are captured or killed on
Provisional Fur Seal Agreement

Canadian land. On the other hand, as I have stated, Canada receives 20 per cent of the total catch from herds on United States territory as compensation for prohibiting Canadians from sealing activities on the high seas.
There is little doubt that these treaty undertakings have saved the Pacific seal herd from extinction. Nearly a million pelts have been taken since the first treaty was signed, but without harmful effect. In 1911 the seal industry was drifting to absolute ruin. Today, because of what has been done through international action, the industry is in a healthy, thriving state and soundly established on a permanent basis.

subtopic: PROVISIONAL AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I crave your indulgence this evening to speak on this bill because I am one of the few, if not the only member who has seen this animal in its natural environment. I have seen the islands which are alike its breeding and1 killing grounds. This treaty was made in 1911 between Great Britain representing Canada, the United States, Russia and Japan. At that time we were at the close of a century during which the fur trade had played a tremendous part in the economy of the world. As hon. members know, Baranoff, the great Russian fur merchant, colonized the Aleutian islands, the Pribilof islands and what is now Alaska. He entered into a treaty with the fur traders of America. As I say, furs played a tremendously important part in the national economy of all the countries concerned and provided a most lucrative business.
The early fur traders built up a kind of mystery around this seal fur trade. They started off by giving extraordinary names to the various branches of their activities. Pelagic sealing means nothing more than the killing of seals in the water. It is a ridiculous name. When citizens of Edmonton come to spend their summer holidays on the gulf islands in my constituency we do not refer to them as pelagic Edmontonians.
I think it would be worthwhile for a moment to investigate the reasons why these treaties were first made. They were made with the

idea of preserving the seals, so that the rich skins might be sold to the aristocracy of Europe and the newly made millionaires of the United States. It was found that you could not control the killing of seals if they were killed in the water. As soon as they come on to their breeding grounds, there is an opportunity for wholesale slaughter of these defenceless animals and there is also an opportunity to control the slaughter.
The seals come on the land for breeding purposes. An old bull seal will collect around him a harem of some sixty female seal cows. Those are not the animals that are killed. Because of the peculiarities of natural history, the younger males have to remain back from the breeding ground, contenting themselves as best they can until they are old enough and are able to entice some of the virgin cows. These are technical names used in the trade.
The younger males are kept back from the breeding grounds until they are old enough to gather a harem. It is at this time that the native Aleuts and Indians drive them away a short distance and knock them on the head. This business of killing is a messy one and very few white men will indulge in it. But it can be regulated and the numbers killed oan be controlled by government inspection, because the carcasses are laid out in rows of tens and hundreds and so forth. It is all controlled; so many are killed each year.
When they are killed in the water there is no control as to what sex of seal is killed. It is quite impossible to distinguish a young male from a young female, and you may kill a mother who has a pup on the land in what are called the rookeries. The mother suckles the baby seal and does not take it out into deep water.
Great destruction was done in those early days. As was mentioned earlier this afternoon, at one time before the treaty was made the herd numbered over 4,000,000 fur seals. Then the indiscriminate killing occurred and the number in the herd dropped down until in 1910 there were no more than 133,000 fur seals. At that time restrictions were put on the number killed and the herd increased, until today it is estimated to be in the neighbourhood of 3,000,000 animals. I want to call the attention of hon. members to that increase since 1910 from 133,000 to 3,000,000 animals.
Why are these animals preserved? That is the big question. They are preserved so that their skins may be sold to make expensive furs for a very fancy trade. It is still a lucrative trade. The last figures which I received from

Provisional Fur Seal Agreement
the department show that in 1947 some 12,289 skins were delivered to Canada as her share and these brought $994,061 in profits to Canada. The question I want to ask is this: At what expense was that $994,061 worth of skins obtained?
I have pointed out that at one time the herd was much larger than it is now, and that it is very much on the increase. These animals live on fish. They are on the Pribilof islands for only a couple of months during the summer when they live on shell fish and decomposed matter. During the rest of the year they range the Pacific ocean, some travelling across to the Siberian shore and others going down the west coast of the continent of America as far as California. While they are moving back and forth they are living on the fish which constitutes the food for the people of this world-fish food that is caught by the fishermen of British Columbia. From estimates which have been made of seals in captivity and by various expeditions which have been carried out by the United States, it has been calculated that the seal herd of a few years ago ate more than the total catch of commercial fishing from Alaska, British Columbia, Washington. Oregon and California. I quote from a report which was produced by Mr. W. McLeod Chapman, who is a biologist of the department of fisheries of the state of Washington. This was published in the California publication, Fish and Game, of October, 1942:
The herd of fur seals now includes more than
2.500.000	individuals. From such data as are now- available it would appear that this herd, at a minimum figure, consumes in excess of
2.500.000	pounds of fish each year in the area from the Pribilof islands to California. This is roughly the annual production of food fish by all the commercial fisheries of Alaska, British Columbia, Washington, Oregon and California.
Millions of tons of small fish are eaten by these animals. A full grown fur seal will weigh anywhere from 350 to 600 pounds. It consumes, so it has been estimated, no less than forty pounds of fish a day, when living on what one might call an austerity diet; that is almost a starvation diet.
We find that Russia has withdrawn from this treaty and Japan has withdrawn from it. Why? Russia has a fur seal herd smaller than the Pribilof herd and it has its rookeries on the Commander islands off the coast of Siberia. There is a smaller Japanese herd off some of the islands off the main islands of Japan. Russia and Japan have withdrawn from this treaty because they realize that these fur seals destroy far more fish than the value of their skins is worth.
5849-212J
There has been in recent years a distinct reduction in the catch of certain types of small fish. I am not suggesting for one moment that a fur seal tackles a full-grown salmon. Oh, no; they eat the smaller fry; they eat the herring; they eat the pilchards. There is a big demand now for herring and a market is opening up again in Asia for the salted herring of British Columbia waters. Those are the type of fish which these marauding animals devour in great quantities. I say that the figures show that there has been a distinct reduction in the number of fish of that type caught in those waters in recent years, in spite of the improved equipment for catching fish of that type. I am not suggesting that the increase in the fur seal herd is the only cause of the reduction in the number of herring that are caught, but I claim that it is very much one of the contributing causes.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, there has been a lot of maudlin sentiment created around these fur seals. It all started when Rudyard Kipling years ago wrote a delightful little story in the "Jungle Book" about a dear little baby fur seal. I suppose every hon. member, when he was a child, saw some performing seal balancing a ball on the end of its nose. Oh, we loved the dear little seal. There have been all these fantastic names to describe the rookeries and the pups. Whoever heard of a pup being born in a rookery? A rookery is where rooks nest. Pups are born on the ground. But all these romantic names, the bachelor bull, the virgin cow, the rookeries and all the rest of it, have been created, with the result that, I suggest, a maudlin sentiment has been built around these poor little animals.
What did we get out of this agreement at an expense equal to the total catch of all the commercial fish on the Pacific coast from Alaska to California? We got 20 per cent of the kill; 20 per cent of the hides that had been cured. Does that give us any employment? Last year, 1947, there were as Canada's share some 12,289 skins. We had no part in the killing or stripping of the carcasses, that was all done by the Americans, done with native labour, by the Aleuts and by the Indians of Alaska. Those hides were shipped past Canadian ports, past Prince Rupert, past Vancouver, shipped in United States bottoms to Seattle, where they were transported by rail. From Seattle we pay the cost of transportation to a United States firm of furriers. Of those 12,000 skins last year, some 8,602 skins were cured in the United States, the remainder, or some 3,687 skins, were cured in Great Britain, in London. No Canadian labour was employed in the curing of those skins. Canada

There is such a thing as free enterprise within one's own country and also free enterprise within the world. I think everyone realizes that at one time five great nations were fighting for the privilege of getting these seals, and it was not found possible for them all to get together and to decide on a proper procedure. It is only recently that Canada and the United States have been able to go in together with a view properly to safeguard the breeding grounds on the Pribilof islands where these seals have been given an opportunity to propagate, and have developed into great herds.
I might say that I feel particularly sorry for the Indians involved. I was not in the house tonight earlier, so that I do not know whether they have been mentioned or not. The fact is, however, that in the early days on the British Columbia coast the taking of sealskins was one of the great means of earning a livelihood for our Indians there. Schooners from Victoria and San Francisco used to call at west coast ports, pick up a load of Indians and their wives, and take them all over the world chasing seals. They would start off at Victoria, and follow them around through the Pribilof islands, across to Japan

and to the Hawaiian islands, calling in at San Francisco and then back home.
It has been found necessary to stop the Indians from sealing on their ancient grounds out there; this is done in the interests of conservation. We find that the Indians are no longer able to go out and catch seals by using their canoes, or boats powered only by hand, or through the use of spears, as was their custom in the old days when the seals were more numerous than they are today.
The thought has occurred to me that these funds which are taken into our consolidated revenue fund might very well be earmarked for the use of Indians, so that in some fashion or another they might be compensated for their loss in revenue which it was their custom to receive.
So far as the amount of good food eaten by seals is concerned, I believe the department has spent a great deal of time in a survey of this subject. I remember in 1936 collecting a lot of seal stomachs for the Department of Fisheries, and it is my understanding that those stomachs were analysed. It was found that only about three per cent of the stomachs showed any trace of salmon, which, after all, is the only commercial fish that would be eaten.
